It observes features of an object and trains a model in the structure of a tree to predict data in the fu‐
ture to produce meaningful continuous output.
Example: a profit prediction model that states the probable profit that can be generated from the sale 
of a product. Here, with the aid of a decision tree regression model, continuous values are predicted. 
A dataset is broken down into smaller and smaller subsets, while an associated decision tree is de‐
veloped incrementally at the same time. A tree with decision nodes and leaf nodes is the final result.
 
Extra Tree Regressor
Extremely Randomized Trees or Extra Tree, is an ensemble machine learning algorithm. Specifically, 
it is an ensemble of decision trees and is related to other ensembles of decision trees algorithms 
such as bagging and random forest.
The extra trees algorithm works by creating a large number of decision trees from the training data 
set. Predictions are made by averaging the prediction of the decision trees in the case of regression 
which improves the predictive accuracy and controls over fitting. Unlike random forest that develops 
each decision tree from a bootstrap sample of the training dataset, the extra trees algorithm fits each 
decision tree on the whole training data set.
CAT Boost
Categorical Boosting or Cat Boost is a machine learning algorithm which can easily integrate with 
deep learning frameworks like Google’s TensorFlow and Apple’s Core ML.
It can work with diverse set of data types and provides best-in-class accuracy. Without extensive 
data training usually required by other machine learning algorithms, it yields state-of-the-art out‐
comes. Boost comes from the gradient boosting machine learning algorithm as this library is based 
on the gradient boosting library. Using different statistics on combinations of categorical features 
and combinations of categorical and numerical features, it transforms categorical values into num‐
bers.
Light GBM
Light Gradient Boosted Machine or Light GBM is an open-source implementation of gradient boost‐
ing designed to be efficient and perhaps more effective than other implementations.
Gradient Boosting refers to a class of ensemble machine learning algorithms that can be used for re‐
gression predictive modelling problems. Light GBM splits the tree leaf wise with the best fit since it is 
based on decision tree algorithms, while other boosting algorithms split the tree level wise or depth 
wise.
The leaf wise algorithm can minimize more losses than the level wise algorithm when growing on the 
same leaf in Light GBM, resulting in much better precision that can rarely be achieved by any of the 
other boosting algorithms. Also, it is very fast, hence the word ‘light’.
XG Boost
The eXtreme Gradient Boosting or XG Boost is a powerful approach for building supervised regres‐
sion models. The objective function contains loss function and a regularization term.
It tells about the difference between actual values and predicted values; that is., how far the model 
results are from the real values. XG Boost is an ensemble learning method. It expects to have the 
base learners which are uniformly bad at the remainder so that when all the predictions are com‐
bined, bad prediction cancels out and better one sum up to form final good predictions. There is lev‐
el wise tree growth in XG Boost.

Precision talks about how precise/accurate the model is. That is, out of the predicted positive, how 
many of them are actual positive.
When the costs of False Positive is high, Precision is the good choice for measure.
Example: In email spam detection, a false positive means that an email that is non-spam (actual neg‐

the precision is not high for the spam detection model.
Recall
Recall calculates how many of the Actual Positives our model captures through labeling it as Positive 
(True Positive).
When there is a high cost associated with False Negative, Recall is the model metric to select the 
best model.
Example: If a fraudulent transaction (Actual Positive) is predicted as non-fraudulent (Predicted Neg‐

Methods of Auto HPO Based on Classification ARIMA
An autoregressive integrated moving average, or ARIMA, is a statistical analysis model that uses 
time series data to either better understand the data set or to predict future trends. A statistical mod‐
el is autoregressive if it predicts future values based on past values.
ARIMA is a good choice if the data is stationary and contains auto correlations with its pervious 
lags.
SARIMA
A seasonal ARIMA model is formed by including additional seasonal terms in the ARIMA. SARIMA is a 
good choice if the data is stationary and has seasonal component in it. We must be careful in choos‐
ing SARIMA over other models when data size is big. 
SARIMA is useful when we have a small dataset and contains a seasonal component in it.
Holt Winter
The Holt-Winters method uses exponential smoothing to encode lots of values from the past and use 
them to predict “typical” values for the present and future. Exponential smoothing refers to the use 
of an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) to “smooth” a time series. It is somewhat dif‐
ferent from SARIMA and ARIMA, as it doesn’t take correlation of previous lags in to account while 
training.
Holt Winter is the go to model if there is strong seasonality or strong trend or both in the data.
STLF
STLF stands for Seasonal and Trend decomposition using LOESS forecasting. This model starts from 
decomposing the time series data with STL decomposition then it fits individual forecasting model on 
the de-seasonalized components it re-seasonalizes the forecasted results with seasonal data to pro‐
duce the final forecasting results.
STLF modeling assumes that a timeseries can be broken down in error, trend, and seasonality 
components.
Theta
Theta Model is basically a simple exponential smoothing model with. Theta Model works well if there 
is strong seasonality or trend or both in the data.
Prophet
Prophet is a procedure for forecasting time series data based on an additive model where non-linear 
trends are fit with yearly, weekly, and daily seasonality, plus holiday effects. It works best with time 
series that have strong seasonal effects and several seasons of historical data. Prophet is robust to 
missing data and shifts in the trend, and typically handles outliers well.
Prophet performs well compared to other models for most of the Time Series Datasets.

TBATS stands for Trigonometric seasonality, Box-Cox transformation, ARMA errors, Trend and Sea‐
sonal components. TBATS is a forecasting method to model time series data. The main aim of this is 
to forecast time series with complex seasonal patterns using exponential smoothing
TBATS is super useful when there are complex seasonalities, at the time it is very slow.
Bernoulli
Bernoulli Naive Bayes is used for boolean data and works on Bernoulli distribution. It accepts fea‐
tures only as binary values like true or false, yes or no, success or failure, 0 or 1 and so on. Example: 
If we want to know that a word occurs in the sentence. It returns a boolean value.
They are extremely fast as compared to other classification models.
Multinominal
Multinomial is a classification task with more than two classes.  Example: To classify a set of images 
with the fruits like oranges, apples, or pears. Multi-class classification makes the assumption that 
each sample is assigned to only one label. That is, a fruit can be either an apple, or a pear; but not 
both at the same time.
Decision Tree
Decision tree builds classification models in the form of a tree structure. It breaks down a dataset in‐
to smaller subsets while at the same time an associated decision tree is incrementally 
developed. The final result is a tree with decision nodes and leaf nodes. Below is a diagram repre‐
senting an example of classification decision tree:
ExtraTree
Extra Trees is an ensemble machine learning algorithm that combines the predictions from many de‐
cision trees. It is related to the widely used random forest algorithm.
It has mostly the same or better performance than the random forest algorithm.
RandomForest
The Random Forest algorithm trains the model using the results of an ensemble of randomly gener‐
ated decision trees. This algorithm creates decision trees on data samples and then gets the predic‐
tion from each of them and finally selects the best solution by voting. This model gives the best re‐
sults when there are non-linear associations between classes. Random Forest is computationally ex‐
pensive but helps in avoiding the problem of over fitting and under fitting.
It is better than a single decision tree since, it eliminates the over fitting by averaging the out‐
come.
Methods of Auto HPO based on Regression
XGBoost
The XGBoost algorithm is used to train the model using the results of an ensemble of randomly gen‐
erated decision trees. The algorithm has a high boosting capability which helps the decision trees to 
improve each other – and makes the model less likely to be a case of overfitting or under fitting. This 
model is generally used when you use many different features to train your model.
LGBM

Light GBM is based on decision tree algorithms. It splits the tree leaf wise with the best fit, 
whereas other boosting algorithms split the tree depth wise or level wise rather than leaf-wise. When 
growing on the same leaf in Light GBM, the leaf-wise algorithm can reduce more loss than the level-
wise algorithm and hence results in much better accuracy which can rarely be achieved by any of 
the existing boosting algorithms.
GradientBoosting
Boosting in machine learning is a way of combining multiple simple models into a single composite 
model. Simple models or weak learners are added one at a time, while keeping existing trees in the 
model unchanged. Decision trees are used as the weak learners in gradient boosting. Each internal 
node of the tree representation denotes an attribute and each leaf node denotes a class label. Gradi‐
ent boost is used to predict a continuous values like age, weight, or cost. Gradient boosting regres‐
sion calculates the difference (residual) between the current prediction and the known correct target 
value. After that gradient boosting regression trains a weak model that maps features to that resid‐
ual.  To the existing model input, this predicted residual by a weak model is added and thus this 
process nudges the model to the correct target. Repeating this step again and again improves the 
overall model prediction.
RandomForest
Random forest regressor is a bagging technique and not a boosting technique. Bagging lets each 
model run independently and then, without preference to any model, aggregates the outputs at the 
end. The trees in random forests run parallel to each other. When building the trees, there is no inter‐
action between these trees. It operates by constructing a multitude of decision trees at training time 
and outputting the class that is the mean prediction (regression) of the individual trees.
ExtraTree
Extremely Randomized Trees or Extra Tree, is an ensemble machine learning algorithm. It is an en‐
semble of decision trees and is related to other ensembles of decision trees algorithms such as bag‐
ging and random forest. The extra trees algorithm works by creating a large number of decision 
trees from the training data set. Predictions are made by averaging the prediction of the decision 
trees. The extra trees algorithm fits each decision tree on the whole training data set.
It improves the predictive accuracy and controls over fitting.

Chi Square
The chi-square test helps to solve the problem in feature selection by testing the relationship be‐
tween the features. Consider a scenario where we need to determine the relationship between the 
predictor variable and target variable. In feature selection, we aim to select the features which are 
highly dependent on the target variable. When two features are independent, the observed count is 
close to the expected count, thus we will have smaller Chi-Square value. High Chi- Square value in‐
dicates that the hypothesis of independence is incorrect. In simple words, higher the Chi-Square val‐
ue the feature is more dependent on the target variable and it can be selected for model training.
MRMR Bayesian Blocks
Bayesian Blocks are used before MRMR for feature binning( continuous numeric features into dis‐
crete values). Since real world data might contain the combination of continuous and categorical 
features, we first bin the continuous features into categorical before performing feature selection 
using MRMR.

2.
Type of Missing Value Imputation: There are 2 modes of Missing Value Imputation which can 
be performed on the data:
•
Univariate: Continuous Features will either be imputed with Mean Value or Median Value 
depending on the skewness of the feature distribution and Categorical Features will be ei‐
ther imputed with Random Sample from the distribution or “Unknown” based on whether 
the target is selected or not.
◦
Multivariate: This mode uses the complete context of the dataset to predict a value to be 
imputed in place of missing values for a given column. Columns with Missing Value are 
considered one at a time, in round robin fashion, and other columns are used to predict the 
missing value corresponding to it.
◦
Method to Handle Outliers: There are 2 modes of operation which the user can choose to 
identify and handle the outliers in the dataset.
•
Clip: In this mode, the user is required to specify the Standard Deviation Bound around the 
mean which needs to be preserved. Data points which are outside the given bound will be 
clipped to the closest bound value.
◦
Winsorize: In this mode, the user is required to specify the percentage of data point which 
needs to be preserved, rest of the data points will be clipped to the closest bound value. 
For e.g. When the user selects to preserve 99% of data: Data points in the Top 0.5 per‐
centile and Bottom 0.5 percentile will be clipped to the corresponding closest bound value.
◦
Categorical Encoding

Bag of Words (BOW): BOW is the simplest technique used to vectorize texts. The general idea is

rence of words in a sentence. Grouping of words more than one word is called n-gram. The

pus. It consists of term frequency which is equivalent to the probability of choosing the word in

Understanding Result Metrics.
6.
The result section provides Antecedents and Consequents items which have occurred to‐
gether in the input data set along with below metrics to define the strength of the relation be‐
tween them.
•
SUPPORT: Frequency of the association and individual items occurring in all transactions.
•
CONFIDENCE: Probability of Consequent being included when antecedent is already 
present.
•
LIFT: The lift metric is commonly used to measure how much more often the antecedent 
and consequent of a rule X->Y occur together than we would expect if they were 
statistically independent.
•
LEVERAGE: Leverage computes the difference between the observed frequency of A and C 
appearing together and the frequency that would be expected if A and C were independent.
•
CONVICTION: A high conviction value means that the consequent is highly depending on 
the antecedent.

Scenarios
SIMBOX Bypass Fraud
Subscriber Identity Box (SIMBOX) fraud occurs when fraudsters team up with international entities to 
route international calls through the internet using VoIP and terminate those calls through a local 
phone to make it seem as though the call made, was local. When a call is routed, a fraudster will cre‐
ate a new route to bypass your internet connection. This means a call is terminated through a SIM‐
BOX. A Fraudster is not visible to you, since the SIM card traffic appears to be normal to an end cus‐
tomer. And operators are cheated by some percentage of revenue.

2.1 Outlier Detection
Removing outlier prior to training results in good prediction. Using the Outlier Detection Operator, 
users can view or remove the outliers by checking IQR or using methods such as DBSCAN and Isola‐
tion Forest. Isolation Forest is used for the Multivariate outlier detection on our Dealer Fraud Dataset 
and based on four features – Number of contracts, Dealer Category, Dealer AIN Days and Total Sales 
count. The dealers which fall on the outlier region are labelled as an Outlier. Isolation Forest tries to 
separate out scattered data points from those which appear closer together.
Based on the number of estimator (Number of trees that will be formed) and contamination (percent‐
age of anomalous points we require), the anomaly data points are found and labelled as outliers.

The machine learning lifecycle consists of many components such as data ingest, data prep, model 
training, model tuning, model deployment, model monitoring, explainability, and much more.
ML OPS
MLOps is focused on streamlining the process of taking the trained machine learning models to pro‐
duction, and then maintaining and monitoring them. MLOps mainly comprises of deploying model, 
monitoring the deployed, and explaining the results given by the deployed model. This enables a 
faster model development, deliver higher quality ML models, and faster deployment and production. 
It also enables us to scale the deployed models easily.
MODEL EXPLANATIONS
The basic goal of model explanations is to describe in detail how ML models produce their predic‐
tion. These help us understanding how it behaves, so they may modify parameters accordingly, to 
improve the model’s accuracy and fix prediction bugs. Some of the model explanations are Counter‐
factuals, Scoped Rules (Anchors), Feature importance (SHAP), etc.
MODEL MONITORING
Model monitoring is the tracking of an ML model's performance after deploying to production. Model 
monitoring loop of any MLOps system, to make sure deployed give the predictions correctly. Over a 
period, the performance of the model might degrade due to many reasons like concept drift, data 
drift, outliers in data, bad data quality, behavioral patterns, seasonal shifts, new regulatory environ‐
ments, market volatility, etc. Hence, we need to monitor the deployed model continuously to avoid 
Counterfactuals
1.
A counterfactual explanation of a prediction describes the smallest change to the feature val‐
ues that changes the prediction to a predefined output. They provide ''what if'' feedback of 
the form ''if an input datapoint were x′ instead of x, then an ML model's output would 
be y′ instead of y''. Counterfactual explainability for ML models “interrogates” a model to find 
required changes that would flip the model’s decision.
•
Feature Importance (SHAP)
2.
Feature importance helps you estimate how much each feature of your data contributed to 
the model’s prediction. This kind of explanation will return a value for each feature called 
SHAP value which describe the contribution of each feature in model prediction. This value is 
the average marginal contribution of a feature value across all the possible combinations of 
features. SHAP value helps to select which feature is important and which feature is useless 
by plotting graphs.
•
Anchor Explanations
3.
The anchors method explains individual predictions of any black box model by finding a deci‐
sion rule that “anchors” the prediction sufficiently. This kind of explanations give rules that 
are followed that lead to a particular prediction. By these rules obtained by the explanations 
we get to know what kind of logic that is followed by the model to obtain the result.
•

DATA DRIFT MONITORING
The change in statistical properties of the independent variables is called Data drift. If there is an ab‐
normal change of distribution between the production data and training data will lead to the false 
predictions. This must be identified and alert the user so that the critical risks can be avoided.

Statistical Rule - Offline
In BMS Query Measure, Enable PR Configuration checkbox is in‐
troduced. It allows to generate the Participating Record (PR) for 
the Batch Pipeline. For more information, see Statistical Rule - Of‐
fline.
Velocity Rule
In BMS SummarizeX, Velocity Rule feature is introduced. This fea‐
ture enables real-time tracking of fraudulent activities by analyz‐
ing the speed and geographical movement of calls within a speci‐
fied time frame. It helps in detecting potential fraud scenarios such 
as SIM swapping, account takeovers, and subscription fraud. For 
more information, see Velocity Rule.
Version History
Version History feature is introduced across different modules of 
the Hypersense. It helps to track and manage different versions of 
the same pipeline.
Enable Validation in Parser
In Data Management Parser, Validation checkbox is introduced to 
check the input file with Record Structure Definition and skip the 
file / records before it is processed. For more information, see En‐
able Validation.
This feature is available for CSV, ASCII and XLS Parser.
Local File Source
In Data Management, Local File Data Source is introduced. It al‐
lows to poll the source file from the local machine. For more infor‐
mation, see Local File.
LDC (Long Duration Call) Op‐
erator
In Data Management, LDC Transformation Operator is introduced. 
It is used to stitch the partial CDRs into single CDRs. LDC picks the 
partial CDR from the Local file source and loads the stitched CDRs 
into data sink. Partial CDR are identified based on the Correlation 
ID associated with each partial record and the LDC Indicator For 
more information, see LDC.
File Reprocessing
In DMS Superset, File Reprocessing link is provided for Collection, 
Transformation Task, Load and Sink charts to process the failed 
files. For more information, see File Reprocessing.

perset
Application Monitoring in context to Superset is added. For more 
information, see:

Flooding Control
In BMS Pipeline Repository, Flooding Control feature is introduced. 
Flooding control is introduced to control the excess case genera‐
tion from the rule engine due to misconfiguration by the user. For 
more information, see Flooding Control.
KPI Decimal Support
In BMS while creating KPI, minimum and maximum field supports 
decimal places. For more information, see KPI Decimal Support.

In BMS under Data Writer, API Sink is introduced. API Sink data 
writer allows you to call the external API(s). It allows you to select 
the API(s) registered within a centralized API framework. For more 
information, see API Sink.

Logs.

In BMS under Transformation Operator, SummarizeX feature is in‐

provements over the existing Summarizer operator as it supports 
watermark configuration, multi-windows intervals, and less mem‐
ory consumption. For more information, see SummarizeX.

In BMS inside Pipeline Canvas, Rerun functionality is introduced. It 
helps to rerun the nodes instead of pipeline and helps to reduce 
the redundancy of the records. For more information, see Rerun.

In Data Management under RDBMS Data Source, you can config‐
ure the database using Oracle, MySQL, and MSSQL. For more in‐
formation, see RDBMS Connector.

introduced. This check allows you to find the duplicate records 
from the file. For more information, see ASCII, CSV and XLSX
Parser.

cale Settings and selected time format is visible in dashboard.

lower case. For more information, see Filter Chart.

External Model Integration
Added support for importing the model built on 
other platforms (Jupyter, Colab) and do live pre‐
dictions on it.
In addition to this, the user can also use func‐
tionalities like "Model Serving”, “Model Explana‐
tions" and "Model Monitoring". 
Auto CASH Operator
Added support for automated model selection 
and tuning for Time Series Forecasting prob‐
lems.
Additionally, user can now perform Auto CASH 
operation on multiple timeseries in a single 
dataset which can be segregated using single or 
multiple columns.
Forecast Operator
Added Bounds around model predictions calcu‐
lated based on historical errors, for indicating 
the Confidence Interval for every prediction 
made by model.
Added support for Forecasting algorithms: SARI‐
MA and Holtwinter.
Added support to perform Sampling internally if 
Sampling operator is not part of the pipeline.
Online FE 
Added support for aggregations on streaming 
data using different types of windows such as 
fixed and sliding.
Operators like Filter, Expression and Summary 
can be used to build new features on streaming 
data for model prediction.
Delta Records
Created new API to store and update the delta 
record information. As part of delta records, we 
are storing the timestamp column and max time 
read when users are reading records from data‐
base using Postgres Reader. Delta record gets 
stored when user runs the pipeline. 
When user converts the training pipeline to mod‐
el scoring pipeline, the delta records information 
stored for training pipeline gets stored for model 
scoring pipeline as well.
When pipeline is running in batch mode, every 
time, we trigger get api to get delta records and 
update accordingly.

File sensor waits for a file to land in a file system. If the path 
given is a directory, then this sensor will return true if any 
files exist inside it (either directly, or within a sub directory).

subsequent operator gets executed, else it will retry for a 
specified number of times.

fails.
•
AutoAIS pipeline names are now displayed in the AutoAIS pipeline 
canvas.
•
AutoAIS pipeline status is now displayed in the AutoAIS pipeline can‐
vas.
•
When the user enters data that has datetime format, AIS now allows 
the user to define the custom format in which the data has been en‐
tered.
•
Once the custom format is entered by the user, the system converts 
the data in the required format.
•
Whenever user encounters an error, there is a Show Details section 
in the pop-up bar which allows user to check the detailed error mes‐
sage being propagated.
•
Set the DataFrame index (row labels) using an existing column. This 
realigns the dataset to be sorted by a new column. This can have a 
significant impact on performance, because joins, group bys, 
lookups, etc. are all much faster on that column.
•
Whenever a new user creates their first AutoAIS pipeline, they are 
given a certificate of acknowledgement from AIS platform.
•
